solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Is sign of hesitation about position leading to confrontation?

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, as in about-face, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: taken as written
er is the noise someone makes while hesitating
a stance is a position or posture

explanation.surface: Someone's hesitant, uncommitted stance seems to be heading for a showdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the verb opening the sentence, but it is fodder for the turnaround along with the hesitation noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Resistance is opposition to someone, which is close in sense to a confrontation or standoff.

clue.text: It's reportedly packaged and sent

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by the sound

parts.note: packaged means wrapped up, which is pronounced the same

explanation.surface: A parcel is said to have been wrapped and posted off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent' looks like posting the parcel, but it is the definition in its old sense of enraptured: RAPT sounds exactly like wrapped.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sent is an old idiom for being transported with delight, entranced, carried away.

clue.text: Politician beginning to speak with queen about international organisation

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter only

parts.note: first letter of speak

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword queen
NATO is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization

explanation.surface: A politician opens a speech beside the queen about a global body.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword's usual queen; the international body sits between her two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A senator is a member of a senate, an elected legislator and so a politician.

clue.text: Sad moralist upset about church putting priests on a pedestal?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters wrap round another piece
something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the eleven letters to be rearranged
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A gloomy moralist is upset that the church elevates its clergy above everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The church abbreviation lands inside the rearranged letters, after their first two. The question mark flags that the definition is descriptive rather than a dictionary gloss.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacerdotalism is the doctrine that ordained clergy hold special spiritual power, which amounts to exalting them above laypeople.

clue.text: Supply help as leading characters

indicators.note: read as supple-y, in a supple or flexible way, so the letters bend into a new order

parts.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to provide assistance in the role of leading actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like the verb to provide, but it is the adverb from supple, meaning flexibly, and signals rearranging 'help as'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, so alephs are characters that lead off the alphabet.

clue.text: Start of Christmas with trading opportunity on the up for light units

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter of Christmas
with and and both join things together

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a sale is a chance to trade

explanation.surface: Christmas lights go up as a shop sale begins in the festive season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the up' governs only the trading opportunity, not the whole string; in a down entry it reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The candela is the SI base unit of luminous intensity, so candelas are units measuring light.

clue.text: A page gone over for homework

indicators.note: something gone over has been flipped over, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: a, as in ten pounds a head, means per
P is the standard abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: A page of a schoolchild's homework has been checked through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' is not just the article here: it stands for per, as in twice a day.
explanation.definitionFit: Prep, short for preparation, is the British public-school word for homework done in the evening.

clue.text: What's authentic about modern library facility?

indicators.note: about means around, so one word encloses another

parts.note: authentic means real or genuine
modern means new

explanation.surface: Someone asks what is genuinely up to date about a library's amenities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facility' here means a service the library offers, not a building or room.
explanation.definitionFit: Libraries let borrowers extend a loan, called a renewal, which is one service they provide.

clue.text: Bill's solution penetrates synthetic materials

indicators.note: to penetrate is to get inside, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: a bill is a poster stuck on a wall; the apostrophe-s supplies the plural S
lye is an alkaline solution used in soap-making

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill has a liquid that soaks into man-made fabrics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is a bill pasted on a wall, an advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: Polyesters are man-made polymers spun into fibres for clothing, so they are synthetic fabrics.

clue.text: Flair shown by the old man capturing an iconic fighter

indicators.note: to capture is to hold inside, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: pa is a familiar word for father
taken as written
Che Guevara, the revolutionary whose face is on countless posters

explanation.surface: Father shows style by seizing a famous warrior.
explanation.walkthrough: Che Guevara's portrait is one of the most reproduced images of the twentieth century, hence iconic; 'fighter' points to his guerrilla war.
explanation.definitionFit: Panache is dash and stylish confidence, much the same as flair.

clue.text: Insignificant number getting married in a cathedral ultimately?

parts.note: No. is the abbreviation for number
M is the abbreviation for married
taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: last letter of cathedral

explanation.surface: Only a few couples get married in a cathedral in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it places something inside, but it is simply two letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominal sum or fee is a token amount, so small that it is trivial.

clue.text: Unquestioned supremacy not a condition to set the world alight?

definitions.text: not a condition to set the world alight?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: the state of having nothing to strike a light with

explanation.walkthrough: 'Set the world alight' is an idiom for being brilliant, but here it is taken literally: without matches you cannot light anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Something peerless has no match or rival; a person lacking lighting sticks is literally in a match-free state.

clue.text: Most formal mega-performer, I boxed

parts.note: a star is a top performer

indicators.note: something boxed is packed inside a box, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: the box doing the boxing is a chest
taken as written

explanation.surface: A big star brags of having fought in the ring, in the stiffest terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxed' does double duty: it says I goes into a box, and the box is a CHEST. The surface suggests boxing as a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Starchy describes stiff, prim manners, like a starched collar, so the superlative means the stiffest and most formal.

clue.text: First person said to be tiny

indicators.note: said means spoken aloud, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: we is the first-person plural pronoun

explanation.surface: The very first human is said to have been small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person' suggests Adam, but it is the grammatical first person, here the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Wee is the Scottish word for little, now widely used for something small.

clue.text: Follower's ace lie — time to go before fuss

parts.note: A is the card abbreviation for ace

indicators.note: something told to go is sent away, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: a fiction is an untruth
T is the abbreviation for time
ado means fuss or bother

explanation.surface: A fan's big lie must be dropped before it causes a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time to go' looks like a phrase about leaving, but it instructs removing a T from the lie.
explanation.definitionFit: An aficionado is a keen devotee of an activity, a fan or follower of it.

clue.text: Get fine and quarrel, say, for creating litter?

definitions.note: a gerund phrase standing for the verb

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
a quarrel is a crossbow bolt, a kind of arrow, and 'say' marks it as an example

explanation.surface: Being fined and having a row might be called making a mess, or litter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarrel' wants to mean an argument, but it is the short heavy bolt fired from a crossbow. The clue reads as an instruction: get F and an arrow, and you have the word for producing a litter.
explanation.definitionFit: To farrow is for a sow to give birth to piglets, which is producing a litter.

clue.text: Something big in the drink — a drink swallowed by idiot

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: clot is British slang for a fool
taken as written
cha is a slang word for tea

explanation.surface: A fool gulps down a cup of something, and it is a big deal in drinking terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The drink' is slang for the sea, so the whole first part defines a sea creature; the second 'drink' is tea.
explanation.definitionFit: The cachalot is the sperm whale, a huge animal that lives in the ocean.

clue.text: Prisoner terribly inert, with deprivation no end

indicators.note: terribly means badly done, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: with no end means losing its final letter

parts.note: need is the state of going without

explanation.surface: An inmate is dreadfully listless, suffering endless hardship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inert' looks like part of the description of the prisoner, but it is the raw material for rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: An internee is someone held in custody without trial, usually in wartime, so a kind of captive.

clue.text: Perhaps sinner and saint going out — they often meet in the dark

definitions.text: they often meet in the dark

parts.note: a cur is a worthless scoundrel, one example of a sinner

indicators.note: going out can mean being out of place or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sinner and a saint go out together, as people do secretly after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like lovers meeting at night; it is cryptic for the pair of drapes drawn together each evening.
explanation.definitionFit: Curtains are drawn closed at nightfall, so their two halves come together when it is dark.

clue.text: Makes good wines — merriment in store

indicators.note: something kept in store is held inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: reds are red wines
fun is merriment

explanation.surface: Someone produces fine wines, and there is fun ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes good' looks like producing good wines, but it is the definition, meaning compensates.
explanation.definitionFit: To make good a loss is to compensate for it, and paying money back does exactly that.

clue.text: One small female in here represented?

definitions.text: One small female in here represented?

indicators.note: to represent is to present again in a new form, so the letters are recast

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
female in its small, abbreviated form
the letters to be rearranged with the others

explanation.surface: A little female figure appears in this picture.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the answer: one young female shown in these letters. I and F are mixed in with HERE.
explanation.definitionFit: A heifer is a young cow that has not yet calved, a small female of cattle.

clue.text: Bird enthusiast wanting story heard

parts.note: a fan is an enthusiast

indicators.note: heard means listened to, so the sound counts and not the spelling

parts.note: a tale is a story, pronounced the same as tail

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher wants to hear a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting' is a link here, not a deletion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The fantail is a breed of pigeon, and also a small flycatcher, both named for their spread tails.

clue.text: Fury a reader fails to finish

indicators.note: failing to finish means stopping short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a lector reads lessons aloud in church, or lectures in a university

explanation.surface: A reader is furious at being unable to finish a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fury' looks like rage, but with its capital it is one of the three Furies of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Alecto is one of the three Erinyes, the avenging goddesses known in English as the Furies.

clue.text: Head dismissing learner as fool

indicators.note: dismissing someone sends them away, so that letter is removed

parts.note: loaf, from loaf of bread, is rhyming slang for head
L is the learner-driver plate

explanation.surface: A head teacher sacks a trainee for being an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang 'loaf of bread' means head, shortened to loaf, as in use your loaf. Dropping the L leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An oaf is a clumsy, stupid person, much like a fool.

clue.text: Being unrealistic about claims made by trader and performer?

parts.note: a trader might say 'I deal'
a performer might say 'I sing'

explanation.surface: Someone is taken in by the boasts of a dealer and an entertainer.
explanation.walkthrough: Each figure introduces themselves by their job: 'I deal', 'I sing'. Run together they make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To idealise something is to see it as perfect, an unrealistic view of how it truly is.

clue.text: One of the old people, this writer, requiring editor's intervention

indicators.note: one thing requiring another's intervention has it come between its parts, so one piece sits inside

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as this writer, so me
ED is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An elderly writer needs an editor to step in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old people' sounds like the elderly, but it means an ancient nation. Setters call themselves 'this writer' to mean me.
explanation.definitionFit: The Medes were an ancient Iranian nation, so a Mede is one member of that historic people.

clue.text: Name in past given to soldiers, eg, The Great

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: ago means in the past
N is the abbreviation for name
men are soldiers in the ranks

explanation.surface: An old honorific bestowed on troops, such as 'the Great'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name in past' reads as a historical name, but it means the name abbreviation placed inside a word for in the past.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnomen is an extra name or epithet added for some deed, like Alexander's title the Great.

clue.text: Like some leaves — last bits of the autumn put in box

indicators.note: put in places one piece inside another

parts.note: a crate is a box

indicators.note: the last bits of words are their final letters

parts.note: the last letters of the and autumn

explanation.surface: Fallen leaves at the end of autumn are swept into a box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last bits' takes the final letter of each of two words, not just of autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: Crenate is a botanical term for leaf edges with rounded scallops, a shape some leaves have.

clue.text: Flower carried by glamorous entertainer

indicators.note: what is carried is held within, so the letters sit inside the following words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A glamorous showgirl carries a bouquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom; it is the crossword sense of something that flows, a river. The Ouse is a river in England.
explanation.definitionFit: In crosswords a flower is something that flows, so a river, and the Ouse is one.

clue.text: Crane has wing half visible, one in French river

indicators.note: with only half visible, the other half is gone from view

parts.note: a wing of a building or team is one side

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: the Moselle flows from France into Germany
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A crane shows part of its wing, standing in a French river.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second half of SIDE shows, then I goes into MOSELLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The demoiselle crane is a small, elegant species of crane found across Asia and Africa.
